----- BEGIN PRE-PRODUCTION AUTHOR MANUSCRIPT -----
Title: 

Large Language Models Generate Diagnostic Likelihood Ratios with Low Mean Bias but Wide Dispersion

Authors:

Paul Chong, MD¹, Shuhan He, MD²,³, Kian Samadian, MD², Amal Mohamed, MBBCh², Boyu Peng, MSc⁴, Emma Chua⁵, Cory Rohlfsen, MD⁶, and Brian W. Locke, MD*, MSc⁷

Affiliations: 

¹ School of Osteopathic Medicine, Campbell University, Lillington, North Carolina, USA
² Department of Emergency Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA
³ Lab of Computer Science, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA
⁴ MSDA Program, MGH Institute of Health Professions, Boston, Massachusetts, USA
⁵ Department of Natural Sciences, Pasadena City College, Pasadena, California, USA
⁶ Department of Medicine, University of Nebraska Medical Center, Omaha, Nebraska, USA
⁷ Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care, Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, Utah, USA

Corresponding Author: Brian W. Locke, MD, MSc, Assistant Professor of Research, Shock Trauma Intensive Care Unit, Intermountain Medical Center, 5121 Cottonwood Street, Murray, Utah 84107, USA. Email: brian.locke@imail.org 

Abstract:

Accurate, context-appropriate likelihood ratios (LRs) are needed for Bayesian diagnosis, but empirical LRs are sparse because diagnostic accuracy studies are costly and context-dependent. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can generate LR outputs that align with literature-reported values. We compared LR outputs generated by three OpenAI models (GPT-4o, o3, and GPT-5) with all literature-reported values curated in TheNNT.com dataset. A few-shot prompt was used to elicit numerical LR outputs, and agreement was assessed using Bland–Altman analyses to evaluate mean bias and multiplicative limits of agreement. A total of 700 reported LRs across 30 conditions were compiled, most involving signs or symptoms (59%), historical elements (19%), or test results (16%). All models demonstrated negligible mean bias. GPT-5 had the narrowest 95% limits of agreement (0.26×–3.70×) compared with o3 and GPT-4o. These findings indicate that LLM-generated LRs can be centered near literature values on average, but they are not interchangeable with published estimates for individual high-stakes decisions. Clinical use, including use for unstudied findings, would require prospective, context-specific diagnostic-accuracy validation.

Keywords:

Likelihood ratios, Bayesian reasoning, Diagnostic accuracy, Clinical decision support, Large language models.

Introduction:

Medical diagnosis requires integrating history, examination, and test findings to identify the condition that best explains a patient’s presentation<sup>1,2</sup>. Bayesian reasoning provides a principled framework for this task because it is information-efficient, broadly applicable, and transparent.<sup>3–5</sup>. Instruction in Bayesian methods can improve clinicians’ diagnostic reasoning <sup>6</sup>, yet broader clinical adoption remains modest and many clinicians continue to rely on intuition, heuristics, and pattern recognition.<sup>7,8</sup>

A major barrier to routine Bayesian updating at the bedside is the scarcity of accurate, context-specific likelihood ratios (LRs). LRs quantify how the presence or absence of a finding (history, symptom, examination sign, or test result) changes the odds of disease<sup>3,4</sup>. However, empirical LR estimates require diagnostic accuracy studies, which are difficult to perform and interpret<sup>9,10</sup>. Consequently, reliable LRs for many common clinical findings are unavailable and true likelihood ratios often vary substantially by clinical context<sup>11</sup>. The condition–finding–context space is combinatorially large, so exhaustive empirical estimation of LRs is intractable. For applied Bayesian reasoning to scale, a rapid and sufficiently accurate way to generate or retrieve LR values is needed. 

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence suggest a potential means to generate such provisional values from encoded clinical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on extensive text corpora that capture clinical concepts and associations<sup>12,13</sup>. They can generalize to new tasks through zero-shot or in-context learning<sup>14,15</sup>, raising the possibility that they may recover LR-estimates  from encoded clinical knowledge. There is growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) for diagnostic reasoning, and recent studies show impressive stand-alone performance.<sup>16-18</sup>. Yet integrating these systems as physician adjuncts remains difficult, in part because their reasoning processes are opaque. Expressing model output as an LR would not make the model’s internal computation transparent, but it would make the claimed odds-updating factor explicit, inspectable, and replaceable within a Bayesian pipeline. 

<sup>3,4,27</sup> Before LLM-generated LRs can be considered for settings where empirical values are missing, a necessary first step is to test whether they align with existing literature-reported LRs. In this study, we evaluated successive generations of LLMs to determine how closely their generated LR outputs align with published values, and to explore whether AI-generated LR outputs can serve as credible, inspectable surrogates for empirical diagnostic evidence. 

Methods:

Study Design:

We conducted a retrospective comparative study assessing the agreement between diagnostic LRs generated by three LLMs and all empirically estimated LRs reported by theNNT.com (© The NNT Group, 2010–2022).  

Data Sources: 

On April 1, 2025, we compiled a reference-standard dataset of all likelihood ratios (LR<sub>Reported</sub>) from theNNT.com, a curated repository of diagnostic likelihood ratios from the published medical literature. When theNNT reported both LR+ and LR− for a given finding, we treated them as separate condition–finding entries corresponding to the finding being present/positive (LR+) versus absent/negative (LR−); both are strictly positive quantities (LR− values are typically <1). Where theNNT finding text included a specific modality (e.g., CT vs ultrasound) or a test name (e.g., D-dimer), we retained that information verbatim in the ‘Finding’ field. We did not inject additional assay thresholds or operational definitions when such details were not present in the source entry. For each condition, a point estimate of each LR was recorded directly or, when only a range was provided, derived as the geometric mean (e.g., “1–2” recorded as 1.41; “1.5 [95% CI 1–2]” recorded as 1.5). LRs were initially extracted using an automated script and then manually validated with duplicate independent review (PC and BWL). Each LR was categorized as a patient historical element, a sign/symptom, a test result, an imaging finding, and/or a diagnostic adjudication (e.g. “diagnosis based on ultrasound”). Scores (e.g. Centor criteria for Strep pharyngitis) were counted as each of the constituent findings. We qualitatively describe the strength of findings as strong (LR- ≤ 0.10 or LR+ ≥ 10), moderate (0.1 < LR- ≤ 0.2 or  5 ≤ LR+ < 10), weak (0.2 ≤ LR- < 0.5 or 2 ≤ LR+ < 5), or negligible (0.5 < LR < 2), consistent with prior literature<sup>3,4</sup>. 

Comparator Likelihood Ratios

On August 25, 2025, we generated comparator likelihood ratios with LLMs (LR<sub>LLM</sub>) for all findings listed on theNNT.com using a few-shot prompting procedure. To represent a range of model ages, complexity, and inference costs, we queried three OpenAI LLMs (OpenAI, LP; San Francisco, California, USA) using the OpenAI API: GPT-4o (model release Nov 20, 2024), o3 (release Apr 16, 2025), and GPT-5 (release Aug 7, 2025). The prompt was designed by a single author (BWL) and is fully described in the supplement. In brief, the system prompt defined the LR, ‘P(finding | diagnosis) / P(finding | not diagnosis)’, gave qualitative LR strength descriptions<sup>3</sup>. The model input consisted of a plain-text pair: ‘Condition: <diagnosis>’ and ‘Finding: <clinical finding text>’; these were not encoded as ‘+’ or ‘−’ symbols. The structured output schema required a single finite numeric LR (>0); because both LR+ and LR− are strictly positive quantities (LR− values are typically <1, not negative), any non-numeric, non-finite, or non-positive outputs were rejected and retried using a bounded retry procedure; retry handling and final failures are reported in the Supplement. Example inputs include: ‘Condition: pulmonary embolism / Finding: tachycardia >100 bpm’ and ‘Condition: appendicitis / Finding: no RLQ tenderness.’. When applicable, the finding text includes the diagnostic modality (e.g., ultrasound, imaging, laboratory assay), consistent with how TheNNT summarizes the underlying studies. We used eight (non-reasoning model, GPT-4o) or two (reasoning models, o3 and GPT-5) clinician-provided few-shot examples that were not in the evaluation set. Inference settings were temperature = 0.2 (non-reasoning model) and ‘reasoning effort’ = "medium" (reasoning models); text.verbosity = "low" was applied where supported (GPT-5 only). Internet search was not enabled for any models. No model fine-tuning was performed.

Outcomes, Measures, and Statistical Analysis

The primary outcome was agreement between reported likelihood ratios (LR<sub>Reported</sub>) and LLM-generated likelihood ratios (LR<sub>LLM</sub>) calculated using Bland-Altman analysis<sup>19</sup> on log-transformed LR values because log(LR) is additive under Bayesian updating and corresponds to an odds-updating ‘weight’ for the observed test result.<sup>4,20</sup>. We calculated multiplicative (ratio) limits of agreement, which indicate the range within which LR<sub>LLM</sub> is expected to lie within an x-fold difference of the LR<sub>Reported</sub> in 95% of cases. 50%, 75%, 90%, and 99% limits of agreement are also tabulated in the supplemental materials. We compared models using paired t-test for mean differences (bias) and the Pittman-Morgan test for differences in the width (variance) of the limits of agreement<sup>21,22</sup>. 

Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted by information type (historical element, symptom/sign, examination finding, test result, or diagnostic adjudication), and by direction of odds updating (LR >1, increasing disease odds; LR <1, decreasing disease odds). Welch’s t-test for bias and Levene’s test for differences in width were used because these analyses compare different sets of LR pairs across groups (i.e., independent observations), whereas paired tests were reserved for within-pair comparisons to LR<sub>Reported</sub>. 

Secondary analyses included LR<sub>LLM</sub> calibration, evaluated by linear regression of log-transformed LLM-generated LRs on reported log LRs, yielding the intercept, slope, 95% confidence intervals, and R². Agreement between qualitative LR strength categories (e.g. strong, moderate, weak)<sup>3,4</sup> was also assessed using Cohen’s Kappa with quadratic weights, which penalizes larger category disagreements more heavily<sup>23,24</sup>. As an additional sensitivity analysis, we defined reliability zones using the literature-reported LR: the central zone was 0.2 <= LR<sub>Reported</sub> <= 5.0, and the extreme zone was LR<sub>Reported</sub> < 0.2 or LR<sub>Reported</sub> > 5.0. We also constructed reliability calibration plots with reported log-LR as the outcome and LLM-generated log-LR as the predictor. These plots address the inverse question: given a model-generated LR of a particular magnitude, what literature-reported LR should be expected?

Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05 without adjustment for multiple testing. There was no missing data. All available likelihood ratios from TheNNT.com at the time of data collection were included, defining the sample size for this descriptive analysis.

Ethical Considerations:

This study used publicly available aggregated data and did not involve human participants; therefore, it was exempt from institutional review board oversight.

Results:

Seven hundred LR<sub>Reported</sub> exploring the 30 available medical conditions were compiled from theNNT.com. Signs/symptoms were the most common type of LR (416, 59%), followed by historical element (134, 19%) and test results (110,16% ) 

LR<sub>Reported</sub> values ranged from 0.01 to 145.9, with a median of 1 (interquartile range 0.7 to 2.2) and a geometric mean of 1.21. Figure 1 shows the distribution of LR-strength categories  of the LR<sub>Reported</sub>. Most (n=400) findings offered negligible strength of evidence (0.5 < LR < 2; 56.5%), with the next most common being weak evidence in favor of a diagnosis (n=120, 17.4%), weak evidence against (60, 8.7%) and moderate evidence for (52, 7.5%). Diagnostic adjudication findings were rare (n=8) but had more extreme LR magnitudes (median 2.06; 75th percentile 16.3; 95th percentile 26.3), whereas signs/symptoms were most common (n=416) and clustered near LR≈1 (median 1.0; 75th percentile 2.1) (Supplemental Table 1). Given the small adjudication sample, this comparison is descriptive.

Three sets of LR<sub>LLM</sub> were generated (for GPT-4o, o3, and GPT-5) for each of the 700 LR<sub>Reported</sub>. Figure 2 shows the 95% multiplicative limits of agreement. All 3 models showed minimal mean bias (GPT-4o 1.02x, o3 0.99x, GPT-5 0.99x; no differences in pairwise comparisons). LR outputs from GPT-5 had the narrowest limits of agreement to the values reported on theNNT.com (95% limits of agreement from 0.26x to 3.7x, P < .001 vs both o3 and GPT-4o ), followed by o3 (0.23x to 4.28x), and GPT-4o (0.23x to 4.53x, P = .58 for o3 vs GPT-4o). Other coverage ranges (50, 75%, 90%, and 99%) are presented in the supplementary materials. Visual ‘striations’ in some panels likely reflect discretization/rounding to preferred numeric outputs under constrained prompting; directional bias is more directly assessed by mean bias and calibration slope.

Figure 3 shows the limits of agreement by finding type. Model-generated evidence-strength outputs followed similar patterns across models. Generated LR outputs for signs/symptoms, historical elements, and imaging findings were similarly close to reported values, while test-result outputs agreed less closely with reported LRs. 

When analyzed by the direction of odds updating (LRReported<1 vs LRReported>1), the overall near-zero mean bias was not explained solely by pooling values on opposite sides of 1.(Supplemental Figure 1).  For GPT-4o, mean bias differed between negative (LR<sub>reported</sub> < 1) evidence (mean 1.13x) vs. positive (LR<sub>reported</sub> > 1) findings (mean 0.92x, P < .001). No difference in mean bias was observed for o3 (0.95x vs. 1.03x; P = .15). GPT-5 showed the opposite pattern of mean bias (negative evidence 0.88x vs positive evidence 1.12x; P < .001). The width of the limits of agreement did not differ by evidence direction for any of the models (GPT-4o P = .11; o3 P = .40; GPT-5 P = .37).

Calibration plots are shown in Supplemental Figures 2a-c. Across models, calibration slopes on the logarithmic scale indicated shrinkage toward neutrality, with GPT-5 showing the narrowest limits of agreement but the lowest calibration slope. Together, these metrics indicate that GPT-5 had lower overall dispersion but greater shrinkage of extreme LR values toward 1.0.

Reliability calibration plots showed that high or low LLM-generated LRs generally corresponded to high or low literature-reported LRs, but with regression toward the center. Reliability slopes were 0.73 for GPT-4o, 0.88 for GPT-5, and 0.76 for o3, with R² values of 0.65, 0.68, and 0.64, respectively. These inverse calibration results indicate preservation of ordinal signal with regression toward the center.

Using prespecified reliability zones based on literature-reported LR, the central zone (0.2 <= LR<sub>Reported</sub> <= 5.0) included 585 rows and the extreme zone (LR<sub>Reported</sub> < 0.2 or > 5.0) included 115 rows for each model. Across models, median absolute log error was 0.18 to 0.42 centrally versus 0.57 to 0.59 in the extreme zone; RMSE_log was 0.57 to 0.71 versus 0.99 to 1.07; and calibration slopes were 0.83 to 1.14 centrally versus 0.74 to 0.78 at the extremes. For GPT-5, median absolute log error increased from 0.18 to 0.59 and RMSE_log from 0.57 to 1.07, while calibration slope was 0.83 centrally and 0.74 at the extremes. Errors were larger in the extreme zone, consistent with greater compression toward neutrality.

Agreement between qualitative evidence categories was moderate for all models (Supplemental Figures 3a-c).<sup>25</sup> The quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ for GPT-5 was highest (0.775, 95% CI 0.728-0.821), followed by o3 (0.745, 95% CI 0.702 – 0.789), and GPT-4o (0.734, 95% CI 0.691 – 0.778).

Discussion:

In this benchmark against 700 literature-reported likelihood ratios across 30 conditions, LLM-generated LR outputs were centered near reported values but showed wide item-level dispersion.  Among the three models, GPT-5 demonstrated the closest agreement with literature-reported values (95% limits of agreement 0.26×–3.70×) and substantial LR-strength category agreement (κ = 0.78), but these limits still imply several-fold disagreement for individual findings. Agreement varied by finding type, with laboratory test results showing looser agreement than history, signs/symptoms, or imaging results. Collectively, these results support a narrow interpretation: LLM outputs preserve the broad ordering and coarse magnitude categories of literature-reported LRs, but individual outputs are not pointwise substitutes for empirical LR estimates. This distinction matters when one result is used to decide whether the post-test probability crosses an action threshold. For example, at a pretest probability of 0.50, an LR of 1.0 leaves the post-test probability at 0.50, whereas an LR of 4.0 raises it to 0.80, a difference that could plausibly change management. 

Prior work shows that AI can complement human diagnostic reasoning by offering distinct strengths.<sup>26</sup> In the present study, LLM-generated LR outputs were not precise enough to substitute for empirical estimates, but they may still have value as provisional inputs for lower-risk uses. In education, such outputs could help trainees practice Bayesian updating and examine how individual findings shift disease probability. In research planning, model-generated LRs could help identify findings for which empirical estimates are absent, uncertain, or discordant, thereby prioritizing future diagnostic-accuracy studies. For diagnostic-accuracy research, model-generated LR outputs could also serve as prior hypotheses, helping identify candidate findings, anticipate plausible LR ranges, and inform sample-size or Bayesian design assumptions before empirical validation.<sup>27,28</sup> Use in clinical decision support would require prospective, context-specific validation before deployment.

This study, to our knowledge, provides the first large-scale evaluation of 700 finding–condition pairs across 30 conditions, resolving LLM clinical reasoning into a quantitative unit: the LR. Unlike end-to-end diagnostic answer<sup>17</sup>, quantitative LR output makes the claimed odds-updating factor explicit and available for clinician inspection, substitution, or recalculation within a Bayesian workflow. This does not make the model’s generation process transparent, but it makes the downstream reasoning step more inspectable. 

Whether the observed limits of disagreement are acceptable depends on their intended use.  The limits of agreement are too wide for individual model-generated LRs to substitute for empirical estimates when one finding is used to decide whether a post-test probability crosses an action threshold. A separate future use case is serial Bayesian updating across multiple findings, in which log-LRs are added on the log-odds scale; for example, estimating the probability of pulmonary embolism by updating with symptoms, heart rate, and D-dimer results. Low mean log-bias is relevant to evaluating such workflows, including simplified approaches that assume conditional independence among findings,<sup>29</sup> but this study did not validate combined posterior estimates. Future work should test how dependence between findings, correlated model errors, and clinical decision thresholds affect performance.

A primary contribution of this work is that it isolates one component of diagnostic reasoning: the LR. Prior studies show that LLMs can match or exceed clinician performance in structured pretest estimation tasks.<sup>31</sup> Framing LLM output as an explicit odds-updating factor makes the downstream reasoning step more inspectable than an end-to-end diagnostic answer, although this study did not compare LR-based workflows with end-to-end LLM diagnostic answers.

We used a reproducible evaluation methodology across a broad set of comparators and multiple model generations and quantified agreement of both qualitative categories and continuous metrics. These approaches gave a consistent picture: model outputs were broadly aligned with reported values but remained too dispersed for pointwise substitution. Interestingly, using long-standing qualitative strength of evidence classification <sup>3</sup>, most of the LRs studied represented “negligible or weak evidence”, underscoring that many single clinical observations shift disease probability only modestly.

Several limitations warrant mention. First, this benchmark cannot distinguish whether agreement reflects de novo inference, distributional familiarity, memorization, or prior exposure to TheNNT or its source literature during model training. Internet access was disabled during querying, but this does not exclude pretraining contamination.<sup>30</sup> Accordingly, these results demonstrate agreement with previously reported LR values; they do not establish that LLMs can reliably generate LRs for novel, unpublished, minimally studied, or context-shifted findings.

An exploratory perturbation analysis provided limited evidence against rigid anchoring to the original source values. When GPT-5 was queried using threshold variants of selected laboratory and imaging findings, outputs changed across thresholds in most finding families, and none met the prespecified criterion for anchoring. However, responses were not consistently monotonic, and the analysis was small and single-run. We therefore interpret perturbation testing only as a sensitivity check: threshold responsiveness does not distinguish de novo inference from memorized or distributionally familiar associations.

We did not manually extract LR confidence intervals, patient spectrum, study setting, reference-standard details, or assay definitions from the primary sources compiled by TheNNT.com Therefore, the comparator values include unmeasured uncertainty, and prompts lacked the clinical detail necessary to reproduce study-specific LRs.<sup>11 </sup> Our results should be interpreted as agreement with theNNT’s curated summaries under minimal-context prompting,  not as study-specific LR replication across defined study protocols or clinical settings. This is important because LR values may vary substantially with patient spectrum, setting, assay threshold, and test implementation.<sup>10,11</sup> 

Prompt design may also have influenced model behavior. We did not perform a prompt-ablation experiment removing qualitative LR-strength guidance. Such an experiment would require a prespecified rerun with stable model versions and repeated sampling, because a single post hoc rerun could conflate prompt effects with stochastic variation or model-version drift. Qualitative LR-strength bands may therefore have contributed to anchoring or shrinkage toward neutrality, and future benchmarks should compare otherwise identical prompts with and without categorical LR guidance.

Laboratory findings appeared particularly vulnerable to disagreement. To characterize this descriptively without primary-study abstraction, we added a supplemental table of the ten largest GPT-5 discrepancies among lab-like test-result findings using only the curated finding text. Five included an explicit numeric threshold or comparator, three included a unit, and six had extreme reported LRs (<0.2 or >5.0). We did not assign causal failure categories because doing so would require abstraction of the underlying diagnostic-accuracy studies. These findings suggest that laboratory LRs may require more precise threshold, unit, and assay information than history or examination findings; when those details are absent or simplified, LLM-generated LRs may regress toward common clinical associations rather than reproduce study-specific diagnostic performance.

We did not quantify within-model stochasticity or provide uncertainty intervals for individual LLM-generated LR outputs. Repeated sampling under controlled settings , including fixed prompts, fixed model versions, and consistent inference settings could estimate output variability for each finding. Future work should evaluate test–retest variability across runs, accounts, model versions, and prompt variations. 

We evaluated one finding at a time, consistent with the conventional definition of an LR for a single observation or test result. Multi-finding prompts would pose a different problem: estimating joint likelihoods and dependence among findings rather than assigning separate LRs to individual components. Because there is no established reference standard for arbitrary combinations of clinical findings, we did not evaluate multi-finding prompts here. Future work should compare structured multi-finding LLM outputs with validated multivariable diagnostic models and with formal Bayesian workflows that specify dependence assumptions.

The critical next question is prospective: can LLMs generate likelihood ratios for findings not already represented in the published diagnostic accuracy literature  and anticipate the results of future diagnostic-accuracy research? Addressing this will require leakage-controlled, preregistered benchmarks with embargoed targets to test true predictive ability.<sup>17,18,30</sup> Future work should evaluate whether richer context improves precision, whether model errors resemble clinician errors, and whether uncertainty can be quantified through repeated sampling, model-version comparisons, or calibrated ensembles. Comparative studies against clinicians and implementation studies in clinical workflows may eventually be warranted, but only after prospective benchmarks show that model-generated LRs are accurate enough for the intended use. The present results are best interpreted as evidence of structured but noisy agreement with reported LRs; they justify further validation, not clinical deployment.<sup>16,31,32</sup>

Conclusion:

LLM-generated LRs in this benchmark showed low mean log-bias and structured agreement with  literature-reported values, but wide item-level dispersion. These findings support further study of LLMs as sources of provisional, inspectable LR outputs for research, education, and hypothesis generation, but not as substitutes for empirical diagnostic-accuracy studies. They should not be interpreted as validation for clinical decision-making, even with analogous published findings. In particular, they do not support generating LRs for unstudied findings outside prospective diagnostic-accuracy research.

Author Contributions:

P.C., B.W.L, and S.H. designed the study. P.C. and B.W.L. compiled the reference dataset from TheNNT.com, performed duplicate independent validation of extracted likelihood ratios, and categorized findings. B.W.L. designed the prompting procedure for large language model likelihood-ratio generation. P.C. and B.W.L. performed the statistical analyses and generated the figures. S.H., K.S., A.M., B.P., E.C., and C.R. contributed to interpretation of the results and critically revised the manuscript. B.W.L. supervised the project. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.

Figure legends:

Figure 1: Distribution of likelihood ratios reported in the literature, as collected from theNNT.com. Background shading represents strong, moderate, weak, and negligible strength of evidence categories<sup>3,4</sup>. Most of the LR<sub>reported</sub> cluster near 1, showing they offer negligible or weak evidence. 

Figure 2: Agreement between literature-reported and LLM-generated likelihood ratios: Each panel shows the agreement between reported and model-generated likelihood ratios (LRs). The Bland-Altman differences were computed on log-transformed LRs and displayed after exponentiation as reported/model LR ratios; therefore, no bias corresponds to unity. The y-axis shows the ratio of LRs (reported/model), and the x-axis shows the geometric mean of paired LRs. Solid black lines represent mean bias; Dashed lines indicate the multiplicative (i.e. x-fold) range in which 95% of LLM-generated values would be expected to be from a value reported on theNNT.com. Narrower coverage intervals represent closer agreement, and deviations of the mean line from unity indicate systematic bias. Shaded areas indicate the confidence intervals on each bound of agreement. All models showed negligible bias. GPT-5 had the tightest agreement with reported likelihood ratios. 

Figure 3: Agreement between LLM-generated and literature-reported likelihood ratios by type of clinical finding. Rows represent clinical finding categories (laboratory, imaging, history, sign-symptom, and diagnosis); columns represent LLM versions (GPT-4o, o3, and GPT-5). Categories were assigned by manual review, and likelihood ratios could be categorized as multiple types (e.g. scores integrating multiple findings).
